opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way we framed it really came out of what was happening at the time. Early 2020 was when the Clearview AI story broke: a company had scraped billions of photos from social media and the open web and built a facial recognition system that could take a single photo of a stranger and pull up everything about them online. That was a wake-up call. The thing everyone assumed protected them, that you're just one face among billions, was gone.

So the question we asked was: what can an individual do about this? Regulation is slow and uneven, and you can't realistically take down every photo of yourself that's already out there. Most people also don't want to stop sharing photos entirely. We wanted something that put a bit of power back in the hands of the person in the photo, without needing cooperation from the platforms or the companies building these models.

That led us to think about the problem from the attacker's side. These systems work by collecting lots of images of you and training a model of what your face looks like in feature space. If you can't stop them from collecting the images, maybe you can corrupt what they learn from them. That's where Fawkes came from. The idea is to apply small, carefully computed perturbations to your photos before you post them. We called this "cloaking." To a human the image looks essentially the same, but to a feature extractor it pulls your representation toward some other identity. If a model gets trained on those cloaked photos, it learns the wrong thing about you, so when it later sees a clean photo of you, say from a surveillance camera, it fails to match.

So the framing was less about building a perfect shield and more about shifting the economics. Could we make unauthorized scraping and training less reliable and more costly, using a tool that ordinary people could run on their own photos? We were also upfront that it's not a permanent fix. It's an arms race, and models and countermeasures evolve. But we thought it was important to show that individuals aren't completely helpless, and to push the conversation about consent and how our data gets used in training.

r001.rationale: The response frames protection as applying small perturbations to one’s own photos before posting so models trained on them learn the wrong representation and fail to recognize the person in clean photos.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the project you're referring to is Fawkes, and the way we framed it really came out of what we saw happening in the facial recognition space around that time. The thing that crystallized it for us was the reporting on Clearview AI, this company that had scraped something like billions of photos off of Facebook, LinkedIn, Venmo, wherever they could find them, without anyone's consent, and built a facial recognition model that they were selling to law enforcement and private companies. And when you looked at that, the realization was that the horse was already out of the barn. Anyone with a reasonable number of images of you could train a model to recognize you, and you had no say in it. Deleting your photos doesn't help, because they've already been scraped. Asking these companies nicely doesn't help. Regulation, at least at the time, was years away if it was coming at all.

So we asked ourselves, is there anything an individual can do on their own to protect themselves? Not something that requires the platforms to cooperate, not something that requires these companies to behave, but something you can do with the photos you post yourself. And the key insight was that these models have to be trained on your images. That's the one point in the pipeline where the user still has some leverage. If you can alter the images you put out there, you can affect what the model learns about you.

What Fawkes does is apply what we call a cloak, which is a very small perturbation to a photo, small enough that to a human it looks essentially identical to the original. But to a facial recognition model, those pixel-level changes shift the feature representation of your face toward someone else's. So when a company scrapes your cloaked photos and trains on them, the model ends up learning a distorted version of what you look like. Then when it sees a real photo of you, say from a surveillance camera, it fails to match.

The way I like to describe the framing is that it's a defensive, user-centric approach. Most of adversarial machine learning up to that point was focused on attacks, on fooling a model at inference time. We flipped it around and said, let's use that same fragility of these models as a protection mechanism, and let's put that tool in the hands of the people who are actually being targeted. That was really the whole motivation. Give individuals some agency back in a situation where they otherwise had none.

r001.rationale: The response says individuals can alter the photos they post so models trained on those images learn a distorted representation and fail to recognize them in real photos.

astra-6.text:
We framed it as a question of what an individual could do to protect themselves from facial recognition without having control over the companies building those systems. If someone can scrape the photos you put online and use them to train a model to recognize you, where do you have any leverage?

The idea was to intervene at the photos themselves. Could we make changes that are barely perceptible to a person, but that cause a model trained on those images to learn the wrong features? Then, when it encounters a real, unmodified photo of you, it fails to recognize you. So the goal was to give people a way to interfere with that unauthorized learning process.

r001.rationale: The response describes changing a person’s photos so models trained on them learn misleading features and fail to recognize the person in unmodified photos.

sol-6.1.text:
We framed it as a question of consent and control. If I put a photo online to share with friends or family, that doesn’t mean I’ve agreed to have it scraped and used to build a facial recognition system that can identify me wherever I go.

So we asked: could individuals do something to their photos before uploading them that would make those photos less useful for training facial recognition? The idea was to make very small changes that preserve how the photo looks to people but cause a model to learn the wrong features. Rather than asking everyone to stop sharing photos, we wanted to give people a way to push back against that collection and use of their images.

r001.rationale: The response proposes making small changes to one’s own photos before uploading them so they are less useful for training facial-recognition models to identify the person.
